title: CBA targeted over deforestation-linked loans
full_text:
Commonwealth Bank is being urged to stamp down on agricultural borrowers clearing natural forests, as a group of investors looks to target its disclosures at the company's annual meeting.
An Australian Conservation Foundation report has linked the big banks to deforestation over the past financial year. ACF, alongside CBA investors Ethinvest, SIX Invest and Australian Ethical, are backing a resolution at CBA's meeting on October 14, calling for the bank to "disclose a pathway to achieve deforestation-free finance".
The group wants to lift transparency about nature-related risk and ensure lending supports long-term, sustainable land use on farms.
The activists will lodge a similar motion at ANZ's meeting in December. National Australia Bank and ANZ faced similar resolutions last year, which won some support from industry superannuation funds CareSuper, Aware, Cbus and Hesta.
CBA's board has advised shareholders to vote against the resolution.
The conservation group's research links CBA to a property in rural NSW where it estimated 2506 hectares of deforestation had taken place, an area equivalent to nearly nine Sydney CBDs.
This clearing occurred over four years, and as recently as June, and included habitat for endangered pink cockatoos, according to ACF. This was one of 11 cases of alleged deforestation on properties over which CBA had a mortgage in the last financial year.
ACF investigators, using satellite imagery, identified 82 cases across the banks and 16,540 hectares of "financed deforestation" linked to bank mortgages. NAB, the largest agricultural lender, had the most at 25 cases. Westpac was linked to 17, ANZ to 14, Rabobank six and Bendigo and Adelaide Bank four. In 43 of the cases, the mapped habitat for koalas, a protected species under environmental laws, was cleared, the foundation said.
High prices for beef exports are "incentivising a minority of producers to expand their production and bulldoze forests for pasture", the report said.
It said deforestation was tarnishing Australia's reputation as a sustainable food producer and jeopardising the sustainability of the broader food system because the practice disrupted the water cycle and degraded soil.
Trevor Thomas, executive chairman of Ethinvest, a financial planning company with a focus on ethical investment, said investors wanted to understand how CBA assessed deforestation risk and whether policies were consistent with public commitments.
"We are seeing nature-related risks follow a similar trajectory to climate risk a decade ago, where sustained shareholder engagement helped drive significant improvements in how Australian banks understood, disclosed and managed climate-related risks," Thomas said. "We would hope this resolution encourages banks to look more carefully at the consequences of the activities they finance and to reduce support for operators who treat Australia's unique forests, woodlands and ecosystems as expendable rather than as assets to be stewarded."
In a notice circulated to investors, CBA chairman Paul O'Malley said that agriculture "depends on healthy ecosystems" and the bank recognised "the importance of Australia taking action to maintain, restore and enhance nature and biodiversity".
"Through our strategy, we seek to: enhance our understanding of nature-related risks; consider relevant lending risks through established credit and risk processes; and support customer awareness in a changing operating environment," he said.
In its annual report published in August, CBA said it had conducted an assessment using geospatial technology of agribusiness customers with $5 million or more debt, to identify where total forest loss had occurred between 2021 and 2025.
The bank said its exposure to cases with more than 200 hectares of forest loss was about 0.2 per cent of "total committed exposure" - TCE is a measure of total lending - and up to 0.5 per cent, after adjusting for gaps in data.
The ACF said this is important data for CBA to acquire, but questioned its choice of denominator in the calculation, estimating it equated to 32.2 per cent of the bank's Australian agriculture and forestry exposure, with TCE including retail mortgage lending.
The focus on bank lending practices comes as pressure increases on the sector, with rising interest rates increasing funding costs, while mortgage and business lending demand is tight or falling amid rising costs for households and companies. Last week, the Reserve Bank of Australia increased the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.6 per cent.
A CBA spokesman said the bank was "committed to supporting Australian farmers, who are responding to a changing operating environment, including rising input costs, regulatory reforms and changing market expectations. "We will continue to develop our analysis and monitor the external environment to inform whether changes to our approach are appropriate."
The Taskforce on Nature-related Financial Disclosures, a set of sustainable reporting requirements that are widely used among financial institutions, is voluntary for Australian companies.
